--------
Robinhood co-founder and CEO Vlad Tenev sits down with DJ Vlad for a wide-ranging VladTV interview on his path from immigrant kid to fintech leader. Tenev reflects on being born in Varna, Bulgaria, moving to America in 1992, and watching his father’s academic journey from the University of Delaware to the University of Maryland after the fall of the Berlin Wall. He also discusses learning English, adjusting to U.S. schools, and eventually studying math at Stanford before leaving UCLA’s PhD track with a master’s degree.

The conversation also introduces Baiju Bhatt, Tenev’s Stanford friend and future Robinhood co-founder, and traces the early mindset that led Tenev toward launching two stock-trading companies before building the commission-free trading app with nearly $400 billion in platform assets. From Stanford, UCLA, Bulgaria, and immigrant ambition to fintech disruption, this interview explores the roots of one of Silicon Valley’s biggest finance stories.

Vlad interviews Vincent Marino about the Patriarca crime family, also known as the Boston Mafia or “The Office,” tracing its rise under Raymond Patriarca Sr., ties to Providence, Boston, and the Dunes Hotel in Las Vegas, and the disputed leadership of Raymond Patriarca Jr. Marino also discusses Whitey Bulger, FBI informant allegations, John Connolly, Stevie Flemmi, and comparisons to *The Departed*. --------
Vincent Marino sits down with Vlad to break down the power struggle inside the Patriarca crime family, also known as the New England Mafia or Boston Mafia, after the death of Raymond Patriarca Sr. Marino discusses Raymond Patriarca Jr.’s contested leadership, the Las Vegas Dunes Hotel skim allegations, and the rising tensions that led to a violent internal war. He also revisits Whitey Bulger’s role as both Irish mob boss and FBI informant, connecting the story to Boston corruption, Stephen “The Rifleman” Flemmi, and the world later dramatized in *The Departed*. Marino details how figures including Robert Carrozza, Joseph Russo, and Vincent “The Animal” Ferrara were tied to the conflict, and claims FBI agents John Connolly, Michael Buckley, and Robert Callahan helped fuel violence by warning him that Frank Salemme wanted him dead. A rare firsthand account of organized crime, informants, and the Patriarca Mafia war in Boston and Providence.

Charleston White adds his perspective on loyalty, apologies, Adin Ross, Phoenix, Atlanta, and how repairing relationships can open doors in entertainment, hip-hop media, and the creator economy.

Part 1: https://youtu.be/ORHsx5EqZJM
--------
Marine veteran Cody Alford sits down with Vlad to recount the brutal realities he says he witnessed during the Battle of Fallujah, from sniper alleys and rooftop firefights to the chaos of checkpoints on the city’s outskirts. Alford explains how insurgent fighters allegedly used women and children as human shields while coordinating mortar and rocket attacks, and describes the impossible split-second decisions Marines faced in urban combat. He also recalls wounded teammates, a controversial medevac decision, the isolation of a nearly abandoned base, and the killing of local workers who supported U.S. forces. The conversation expands to Ramadi, 2nd Battalion, 4th Marines, School of Infantry, IEDs, foreign fighters, supply routes, and the emotional toll of learning his family had been mistakenly told he was dead. A stark firsthand account of Iraq War combat, leadership, survival, and the aftermath of Fallujah.

recentItems.title: Dale Comstock: I Prefer Shooting From Far Away Because The Kills Are Less Personal (Part 10)
recentItems.description:
Become a VladStocks Member now: https://www.youtube.com/vladtv/join

Part 9: https://youtu.be/H-9s8ix6X8M
Part 1: https://youtu.be/U21AbA_cZII
--------
Dale Comstock sits down with Vlad to reflect on the realities of warfare, lethal force, and the mindset required in combat. The former Special Forces operator discusses why he never kept a body count, recalling a conversation with Chris Kyle of *American Sniper* after meeting him on *Stars and Stripes*. Comstock explains how mortar teams, return fire, and crew-served weapons can blur individual responsibility, connecting it to “group absolution” in World War I, World War II, Vietnam, gangs, and bar fights.

He also revisits his first confirmed shooting near Modelo Prison, describing the split-second decisions involved when civilians were dangerously close. In a candid moment, Comstock explains why engaging from distance feels less personal than close-range combat, where a soldier sees a face, fear, and humanity. The conversation also touches on David Grossman’s *On Killing*, sniper psychology, aggression, hesitation, and the emotional separation many combat veterans rely on to survive.
